title: Beyond slop, taste, and AI moral panic: What social science tells us
gist: Tim Sullivan argues that "taste" is a folk category bundling three separable mechanisms — predicting success, social brokerage, and trained judgment — and that social science says only two survive cheap AI production: inhabiting undocumented social worlds, and apprenticeship structures that train discrimination. The investable conclusion is that the scarce asset in an AI-saturated content economy is not taste but the social infrastructure (audiences, off-record networks, junior-training pipelines) that manufactures it.

themes.theme: Slop panics are a repeating cost-curve pattern

insights.claim: Every historical collapse in media production cost has produced both a flood of derivative content and a moral panic about cultural decline — Grub Street, the penny press, pulp fiction, television, blogging, social media, and now AI-generated content.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: Treat the current "AI slop" discourse as a predictable phase of a cost-curve transition, not evidence that the technology fails commercially; prior panics did not stop adoption of the cheaper medium.
insights.quote: Whenever technology dramatically lowers the cost of producing media, it unleashes a flood of cheap, derivative work — and a chorus of critics convinced that culture has reached a new low.
insights.locator: What I'm saying is, slop is hardly

insights.claim: When execution costs fall and the masses enter a creative market, incumbent elites reliably retreat to claims of superior taste as their defensible differentiator.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: Be skeptical of "taste" as a stated moat in pitch decks for creative and media businesses — historically it is the rhetorical position of the party losing a cost advantage.
insights.quote: Claims to taste become their refuge, and taste achieves apotheosis.
insights.locator: Each time, the cost of execution falls

insights.claim: The 18th-century Grub Street content economy was fully commercial on both sides — single verses, pamphlets, periodicals, and newspapers were produced and consumed for money by respectable people who publicly decried the trade.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: Public revulsion at cheap content has historically coexisted with strong paid demand for it — stated preference against slop is a poor proxy for revenue.
insights.quote: No respectable person would take part in such a dreadful enterprise … except that lots of respectable people did, even while decrying it to their equally titillated friends.
insights.locator: Grub Street produced mountains of what

themes.theme: Disaggregating taste into machine-replicable vs. scarce parts

insights.claim: If taste consists of stable criteria that experts consistently apply, current AI can essentially replicate it, because a model trained on enough Bauhaus objects can infer the principles and a model trained on a literary agent's acquisitions can approximate that agent's editorial preferences.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: Any curation or editorial business whose value rests on consistently applied, articulable criteria is directly exposed to model substitution.
insights.quote: Taste as the consistent application of discoverable rules is precisely the kind of pattern-recognition problem modern AI excels at.
insights.locator: But this immediately raises the question

insights.claim: "Taste" is a folk category into which prediction, judgment, social position, experience, and luck have been collapsed, and AI pressure forces those mechanisms to be pulled apart and priced separately.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: When diligencing a "human judgment" moat, ask which of the five mechanisms is actually operating — only some of them remain scarce.
insights.quote: it’s a folk category into which we’ve collapsed separate mechanisms. AI forces us to disaggregate them.
insights.locator: So what are we really talking about

insights.claim: The useful question is not whether machines have taste but which mechanisms producing good human judgment remain scarce once production becomes cheap.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: Reframes AI displacement analysis around scarcity of inputs rather than capability benchmarks — a cleaner screen for which human roles retain pricing power.
insights.quote: the question shifts from whether machines have taste to which mechanisms that produce good human judgment remain scarce when production becomes cheap.
insights.locator: Drawing on social science can help

insights.claim: Defining taste as simply knowing what is good is tautological, while defining it as personal preference cannot explain why certain people repeatedly identify promising ideas, products, or creators before everyone else.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: Repeatable early identification is an empirical claim that should be tested against a track record and a mechanism, not accepted as innate sensibility.
insights.locator: If, on the other hand, "taste" isn't reducible

themes.theme: Salganik/Watts music lab: success is path-dependent, not quality-determined

insights.claim: Columbia University sociologists Duncan Watts and Matt Salganik built an artificial online music lab in the early 2000s in which thousands of participants downloaded songs by unknown bands across eight experimental groups, with download counts visible in some conditions, hidden in others, and deliberately manipulated in others (for example showing a song at #1 when it was not).
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: This is the canonical experimental evidence that visible social proof, not intrinsic quality, drives winner-take-all outcomes in content markets.
insights.locator: One body of research that may help

insights.claim: In the music lab, hiding social information produced evenly distributed downloads, while showing it caused outcomes to diverge so sharply that a song that became a runaway hit in one world performed poorly in another.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: Platform design choices about exposing engagement counts mechanically manufacture hit concentration — a lever for anyone building or investing in discovery surfaces.
insights.quote: When social information was hidden, downloads were evenly distributed. But when people could see what others were choosing, outcomes diverged.
insights.locator: When social information was hidden

insights.claim: Once quality clears a basic threshold, success is heavily shaped by social influence and path dependence, so domain experts such as TV executives can reliably filter out obvious failures but cannot predict breakout successes among the remaining strong candidates.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: Expert judgment should be underwritten as downside screening, not upside selection — argues for portfolio breadth over conviction concentration in hit-driven categories.
insights.locator: The larger lesson is that once quality

insights.claim: Matt Salganik has stated that the success of Harry Potter was a fluke.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: The canonical mega-hit is used as evidence that outlier returns in content are unforecastable, undercutting any thesis premised on picking the next franchise.
insights.quote: the success of Harry Potter was a fluke.
insights.locator: Or as Salganik has said

insights.claim: Because success is not dictated by quality alone, taste cannot be defined as the ability to predict success.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: Removes prediction from the list of defensible human advantages, narrowing where a genuine AI-resistant edge can exist.
insights.locator: Success is not necessarily dictated by quality

insights.claim: AI's contribution to hit markets is volume — more candidates clearing the good-enough bar than any single curator can sort — which means quality determines even less of which work lands and existing audience or network position determines more.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: Expect the value of pre-existing distribution and audience assets to appreciate relative to the value of content production itself as AI floods supply.
insights.quote: Whichever candidates already have an audience are the ones most likely to catch a wave before the field crowds them out.
insights.locator: Take the socially contingent hit first

themes.theme: Brokerage and structural holes as the residual human edge

insights.claim: Sociologist Ron Burt found across decades of organizational network research that the most innovative employees were rarely embedded in a single tightly knit community but instead occupied "structural holes" — the gaps between otherwise disconnected groups.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: Provides a screenable proxy for innovative talent: map an individual's cross-community reach rather than credentials or raw intelligence.
insights.quote: Here, innovation isn’t a matter of exceptional intelligence but of extraordinary position.
insights.locator: Burt's conclusions grew out of decades

insights.claim: Burt's method was to reconstruct who communicated with whom inside organizations and then compare those communication patterns against promotion, compensation, and managers' evaluations.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: The measurement approach is replicable inside portfolio companies — internal comms graphs can be tied to realized performance outcomes.
insights.locator: Burt's conclusions grew out of decades

insights.claim: What is described as taste may not be an aesthetic faculty residing inside someone's head at all but a structural advantage arising from where that person sits in a social network.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: If taste is positional rather than innate, it can be engineered and hired for deliberately — and it also decays when a person's network position changes.
insights.quote: Their “taste” emerges not from mysterious intuition but from repeated exposure to combinations that no one else is able to see.
insights.locator: This suggests that taste may not be

insights.claim: An LLM trained on everything effectively has access to all networks simultaneously, so if structural holes were purely about information access AI would already dominate brokerage — but the broker's real advantage is tacit, coming from actively participating in multiple communities and accumulating trust and experience that cannot be simulated from training data.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: Locates the durable human moat in relational and embodied participation rather than information arbitrage — relevant to which advisory, sourcing, and dealmaking roles survive.
insights.quote: You can’t simulate being an outsider-insider from training data alone. That’s a defensible human edge — for now, at least.
insights.locator: An LLM trained on, well, everything

insights.claim: LLMs already perform the cheap half of brokerage — surfacing what is happening in an adjacent field to anyone who asks, which previously required actually knowing someone in that field — leaving the question-framing to humans.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: Cross-domain information brokerage as a paid service is being commoditized; price and staff accordingly.
insights.quote: (Someone does still need to know to ask the right questions.)
insights.locator: Brokerage holds up better

insights.claim: The structural holes that will still pay off are those spanning worlds that have not been written down anywhere an LLM could ingest them — subcultures, informal practice, and arguments that happen in a room and never make it onto the record.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: Deal sourcing and research edges shift toward deliberately undocumented territory — off-record rooms, niche communities — because anything indexed is already priced in by models.
insights.quote: If brokerage keeps paying off, it will be because someone sought out exactly that kind of undocumented and undocumentable territory.
insights.locator: Brokerage holds up better

insights.claim: LLMs can already perform the tasks associated with entry-level professional roles — drawing up contracts like a junior law associate, doing basic financial analysis like a junior consultant, and coding like an engineer — which both lets firms cut costs and grants non-experts access to expertise formerly bought at Big Law hourly rates.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: Points to margin compression in billable-hour professional services and a demand shift toward self-serve expertise tools.
insights.locator: LLMs can perform the tasks often associated

insights.claim: Economist Christian Catalini argues the remaining human role in AI-assisted work is verification — making sure the LLM's output did not drift too far, with humans checking and correcting.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: Verification workflow, not generation, is where headcount and tooling spend concentrates in AI-adopting firms.
insights.quote: The human role in all of this, argues economist Christian Catalini, is verification: making sure the LLM’s output didn’t drift too far.
insights.locator: The human role in all of this

insights.claim: Judgment is not innate but accumulated through apprenticeship, feedback, and exposure — illustrated by the author's own training as a junior editor at Princeton University Press, where photocopying his boss's green-fountain-pen edits taught him an editorial style that still underpins his work.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: Senior judgment has a multi-year production lead time; firms cannot buy it back quickly once the training pipeline is cut.
insights.quote: If we are to continue to create humans with taste, we have to create spaces where they can develop it.
insights.locator: Back in the day, when I was a junior editor

insights.claim: Firms that invest in apprenticeships may lose in the short term to competitors who automate aggressively, but the tradeoff resembles overcutting a forest — chopping down every sapling improves one quarter's balance sheet while guaranteeing no mature trees later.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: Aggressive entry-level automation should be read as pulling forward earnings against a future senior-talent shortfall — a quality-of-earnings question for services businesses.
insights.locator: The obvious objection is that firms investing

insights.claim: There is a tragedy-of-the-commons risk in which all firms simultaneously dispense with junior jobs and the entire industry lacks senior judgment later, analogous to a timber company that harvests all the young trees.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: An industry-wide senior-talent scarcity in the 2030s would raise senior compensation and reward firms that kept training pipelines intact.
insights.locator: Firms that simply dispense with entry-level roles

insights.claim: The mechanism that actually built judgment was repeated correction by a senior person, not the grunt work itself, so apprenticeship can survive if junior roles are redirected from drafting from scratch to supervised checking and correcting of AI output.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: The operational differentiator among AI-adopting firms is whether they redesign junior roles as supervised verification or simply delete them — the former captures savings without destroying the talent pipeline.
insights.quote: The process that mattered was “someone catches what you got wrong, repeatedly, until you stop getting it wrong.”
insights.locator: This may be backward

insights.claim: The scarce resource in the age of AI is not taste itself but the social infrastructure — environments rewarding experimentation, networks exposing people to novel combinations, and institutions cultivating discrimination — that produces people described as having it.
insights.speaker: Tim Sullivan
insights.so_what: Directs attention and capital toward the training and network institutions that manufacture judgment, rather than toward hiring for a scarce innate quality that may not exist.
insights.quote: In the age of AI, the scarce resource isn’t taste. What threatens to become scarce is the social infrastructure that produces the people we describe as having it.
